abstract: Nowadays, robotic telemanipulation enables humans to control robots so as to execute tasks in a manner similar to how they perform them, and serves as an essential approach for collecting on-robot data for robot learning by human demonstrations. The quality of collected demonstrations directly impacts the performance of the learned policy. However, existing telemanipulation systems rely heavily on human operation, particularly for large-scale data collection. Collecting dozens or hundreds of demonstrations is a demanding process, as operators tend to fatigue quickly, especially during the execution of dexterous tasks that require sustained concentration. Recently, semi-autonomous robotic telemanipulation has emerged as a promising direction that reduces operator workload while preserving human-in-the-loop control for task execution. We therefore introduce a scalable, intuitive, semi-autonomous robotic telemanipulation system that leverages a mixed reality (MR) headset for on-robot data collection. The system autonomously executes the majority of the task trajectories and only requires the operator to make fine adjustments at key stages. We validate the effectiveness of our system by collecting data and training imitation learning policies on the execution of a high-precision, fine-grained bimanual peg-in-hole task. With lower data collection effort, our system obtains high-quality demonstrations that can be used to train fully autonomous task execution policies.

sections.body: The paper addresses operator fatigue in large-scale telemanipulation for imitation learning. The authors build a mixed reality system on the Apple Vision Pro headset that maps hand gestures to robot end-effector commands in real time, while the robot executes most of each trajectory. The stated target is fine-grained bimanual tasks, where misalignment in one arm accumulates through synchronization with the other. The collected demonstrations train an Action Chunking with Transformers (ACT) policy, which the section uses to test data quality and scalability. The stated aim is to reduce operator workload while keeping human-in-the-loop correction.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Manual telemanipulation fatigues operators during large-scale fine-grained data collection, motivating a semi-autonomous mixed reality system.

sections.body: This section reviews telemanipulation, data collection, and imitation learning. It reports that VR-based and Apple Vision Pro-based systems have been used for dexterous demonstrations, but says these often require considerable operator experience and target relatively simple tasks. Semi-autonomous telemanipulation is reported to improve physical demand, mental workload, and overall experience in complex assembly, based on System Usability Scale and NASA Task Load Index user studies. The authors limit their scope to industrial scenarios where parallel grippers suffice, arguing that fewer degrees of freedom reduce accumulated error. Exoskeleton and mirroring-arm systems are described as relying entirely on manual operation, which causes fatigue. Behavioral cloning, ACT, and Diffusion Policy are summarized as prior imitation learning methods.
sections.heading: Related work
sections.headline: Prior systems demand considerable operator experience, and semi-autonomous control has been tested mainly on complex assembly tasks.

sections.body: The hardware is two 6-DoF UR5e serial manipulators with parallel grippers and wrist cameras, plus a global camera, all managed in one ROS2 node. In Hybrid Telemanipulation (HT), FoundationPose estimates grasp poses autonomously, and the operator then takes full control of the insertion. In Trajectory Execution Control (TEC), the robot grasps autonomously and replays an insertion trajectory from an expert demonstration. Operator input adds displacement increments to that trajectory, and execution pauses while input is detected. Wrist poses from the headset are retargeted to end-effector motion using a scale factor computed at calibration and a low-pass filter. Policy observations are RGB images from three cameras at 480×640 resolution plus end-effector poses, and actions are 20-dimensional target poses with a 6D rotation representation.
sections.heading: Methodology
sections.headline: Two semi-autonomous modes automate grasping, with an operator correcting insertion by hand tracking on Apple Vision Pro.

sections.body: The task is a bimanual peg-in-hole insertion with a 1 mm tolerance, with the enclosure and connector placed at random locations. Three modes are compared: Conventional Telemanipulation (CT), the baseline; Hybrid Telemanipulation (HT), with automated grasping; and Trajectory Execution Control (TEC). Each mode collects 30 successful demonstrations at 50 Hz. The policies use ACT with about 85M parameters, trained for around 6 hours on a single 10GB RTX 3080 GPU, with identical hyperparameters across conditions. Each trained policy is evaluated over 30 rollouts in a fully autonomous mode, with HT and TEC switching to the learned policy after grasping. Success means the connector is fully inserted without dropping.
sections.heading: Experiments
sections.headline: Peg-in-hole experiments compare conventional, hybrid, and trajectory-correction modes, collecting 30 demonstrations per modality.

sections.body: Table II reports demonstration collection: CT succeeded in 30/38 trials (0.78) with average time 35.5±7.21 s; HT 30/39 (0.77), 36.5±5.14 s; and TEC 30/35 (0.86), 41.3±4.81 s. Insertion success was 0.81, 0.91, and 1.00 respectively. TEC reached 30 successes in fewer trials and recorded no insertion failures. Table III reports policy rollouts: CT 1/30 (0.03), HT 20/30 (0.67), and TEC 23/30 (0.77), with insertion success 0.06, 0.74, and 0.88. The authors attribute CT's policy failures partly to limited demonstrations and random object placement, and TEC's longer execution time to pauses during manual corrections. The text notes that CT had few successful trials, so its execution time is defined as the duration until the policy stops outputting updates.
sections.heading: Results and Discussion
sections.headline: Policies trained on trajectory-correction data succeed in 23/30 rollouts, against 1/30 for conventional data.

sections.body: The authors conclude that the system offers a practical balance for industrial applications, scaling demonstration collection while reducing manual effort. They list three limits. The lack of force feedback limits detection of contact states during peg-in-hole insertion, and they propose force/torque sensors during collection. All demonstrations used objects in a facing-up orientation, so flipped objects and switched object positions remain untested. The number of training demonstrations may be insufficient, which the authors say is most evident for the CT modality, and a larger, more diverse dataset would likely improve success.
sections.heading: Conclusions and Limitations
sections.headline: The authors note that missing force feedback, untested flipped objects, and few demonstrations limit the system.
